image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:Ye Olde Trip to Jerusalem - July 2013,.jpg' (1393×1021) confirms Ye Olde Trip to Jerusalem; visually checked on contact sheet. desc: Ye Olde Trip to Jerusalem is a public house in Nottingham which claims to have been established in 1189; however, there is no documentation to verify this date.

facts.one_liner: A whitewashed inn built into the sandstone of Castle Rock beneath Nottingham Castle.
facts.why_go: One of several pubs that claim to be England’s oldest, the Grade II listed ‘Trip’ leans against Castle Rock, and some of its rooms are caves carved straight out of the soft sandstone. The painted date of 1189 on its wall links it to legend of crusaders gathering here before heading to Jerusalem. Inside you’ll find low ceilings, smoke-darkened rock walls and quirky curios, all a short climb below Nottingham Castle.
facts.best_time: Weekday afternoons for a seat in the cave rooms; summer evenings for the courtyard under the rock.
facts.how_to_get_there: Nottingham station is about a 10-minute walk away; the pub sits on Brewhouse Yard at the foot of Castle Rock.
facts.good_to_know: The 1189 founding date is a claim, not documented history. Ask staff about the cellar caves, which are sometimes shown on tours.

facts.one_liner: An Arts and Crafts jewel box of marble, mosaic and bronze friars at Blackfriars.
facts.why_go: This wedge-shaped Grade II* listed pub stands on the site of a medieval Dominican friary, and its early-20th-century makeover by architect H. Fuller Clark and sculptor Henry Poole turned it into one of London’s most extraordinary interiors. Jolly friars appear in bronze reliefs, marble, mosaics and carved inscriptions throughout. In the 1960s a campaign backed by poet John Betjeman helped save it from demolition.
facts.best_time: Mid-afternoon on weekdays, before the City after-work crowd arrives, to see the interior properly.
facts.how_to_get_there: Directly opposite Blackfriars station (Tube and National Rail) on Queen Victoria Street.
facts.good_to_know: It is very busy on weekday evenings with office workers. Tables in the back saloon have the best decoration.

facts.one_liner: A timbered riverside inn on the Thames close to where the Mayflower set out in 1620.
facts.why_go: The Mayflower stands on Rotherhithe Street near the mooring where the Mayflower ship began its voyage in 1620; the ship’s captain, Christopher Jones, is buried at St Mary’s church nearby. The building dates largely from the 18th century, with dark beams, a tiny back terrace on stilts over the river, and a nautical, candlelit interior.
facts.best_time: Late afternoon to sunset, when the jetty terrace catches the light over the Thames.
facts.how_to_get_there: Rotherhithe Overground station is a few minutes’ walk away; Canada Water (Jubilee line) is about 10 minutes.
facts.good_to_know: The riverside jetty is small and fills up fast in good weather. Pair a visit with the Brunel Museum next door.

facts.one_liner: A hidden tavern tucked down a narrow alley off Hatton Garden.
facts.why_go: Hidden down Ely Court, a passage between Hatton Garden and Ely Place, Ye Olde Mitre traces its origins to 1546, when it served the household of the Bishops of Ely; the present building dates from the 18th century. Its wood-panelled snugs are famously hard to find, and in a corner of the bar stands the preserved trunk of a cherry tree that Elizabeth I is said to have danced around.
facts.best_time: Weekday afternoons and early evenings—the pub has traditionally been closed at weekends, so check hours.
facts.how_to_get_there: Chancery Lane and Farringdon stations are each about 5 minutes’ walk; look for the small lamp marking the alley.
facts.good_to_know: Opening days are limited; confirm before visiting. Space is tight, so go in a small group.

facts.one_liner: A 16th-century coaching inn on the edge of Hampstead Heath.
facts.why_go: This Grade II listed inn on Spaniards Road dates back to the 16th century and sits beside an old tollhouse that still narrows the road. Legend links it to the highwayman Dick Turpin, and it appears in Charles Dickens’s The Pickwick Papers and Bram Stoker’s Dracula. The big garden makes it a classic stop after a walk across the Heath or a visit to nearby Kenwood House.
facts.best_time: Spring and summer weekends for the garden; winter afternoons for fireside rooms after a Heath walk.
facts.how_to_get_there: Hampstead (Northern line) is about 20 minutes’ walk across the Heath; bus 210 stops outside.
facts.good_to_know: Expect a crowd on sunny weekends. Kenwood House (free entry) is a short walk away.

facts.one_liner: A low-beamed tavern tucked beneath Oxford’s old city wall.
facts.why_go: Reached through narrow alleys off Holywell Street and New College Lane near the Bridge of Sighs, the Turf Tavern has served drinks since at least the late 18th century, when it was known as the Spotted Cow. A stretch of Oxford’s medieval city wall runs beside its beer gardens. It is a student institution, and it is where future Australian prime minister Bob Hawke famously set a record for downing a yard of ale.
facts.best_time: Autumn and winter evenings, when braziers glow in the courtyards; summer for long afternoons outside.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 15 minutes’ walk from Oxford station; follow St Helen’s Passage from New College Lane.
facts.good_to_know: It is hard to find on purpose—look for the signs at the alley entrances. Food is served most of the day.

facts.one_liner: A Grade I listed Victorian gin palace of mosaics, carved wood and stained glass.
facts.why_go: ‘The Phil’ was built around 1898–1900 opposite the Liverpool Philharmonic Hall, decorated by craftsmen who had worked on ocean liners. It is one of very few pubs listed at Grade I, with a mosaic-floored bar, copper panels, carved mahogany, stained glass and grand rooms named Brahms and Liszt. Its marble Victorian gents’ toilets are themselves a listed attraction.
facts.best_time: Afternoons for a quiet look at the rooms; concert nights at the Philharmonic Hall for buzz.
facts.how_to_get_there: On the corner of Hope Street and Hardman Street, about 15 minutes’ walk from Liverpool Lime Street.
facts.good_to_know: Visitors of any gender may politely ask to peek into the famous gents when it is empty.

facts.one_liner: A village inn beneath Arthur’s Seat with a centuries-old skittle alley.
facts.why_go: In Duddingston village on the far side of Arthur’s Seat, the Sheep Heid claims an inn has stood here since 1360, which would make it one of Scotland’s oldest licensed premises; the current building is largely 18th century. Its historic skittle alley still runs, and visitors are said to have included Mary, Queen of Scots and Robert Burns. It makes a perfect end to a walk over Holyrood Park.
facts.best_time: Spring to autumn, combined with a walk over Arthur’s Seat; the beer garden is lovely in summer.
facts.how_to_get_there: Walk over Arthur’s Seat from Holyrood (about 45 minutes) or take bus 42 to Duddingston.
facts.good_to_know: Book the skittle alley ahead for groups. Duddingston Loch and Kirk are next door.

facts.one_liner: A Victorian island bar ringed with Royal Doulton tile portraits of inventors.
facts.why_go: Behind an 1860s façade on West Register Street, the Café Royal keeps one of Edinburgh’s finest Victorian interiors: an island bar, ornate plasterwork, and large Doulton ceramic tile pictures of inventors such as James Watt and George Stephenson. The adjoining Oyster Bar has stained-glass windows showing sportsmen and is a classic place for seafood.
facts.best_time: Any time of year; weekday afternoons are calmest for admiring the tiles.
facts.how_to_get_there: Just off the east end of Princes Street, a few minutes from Edinburgh Waverley station.
facts.good_to_know: The Oyster Bar restaurant gets booked up; reserve ahead for dinner.

facts.one_liner: A lonely slate coaching inn on Bodmin Moor, famous from Daphne du Maurier’s novel.
facts.why_go: Built as a coaching inn in 1750 on the old road across Bodmin Moor, Jamaica Inn has long been associated with smuggling, and it inspired Daphne du Maurier’s 1936 novel Jamaica Inn. Today it combines a beamed bar, rooms and a smugglers museum, and makes a dramatic base for walks to Brown Willy and Dozmary Pool.
facts.best_time: Late spring to early autumn for moorland walks; misty winter days for full atmosphere.
facts.how_to_get_there: Just off the A30 at Bolventor, roughly halfway between Launceston and Bodmin; a car is easiest.
facts.good_to_know: It is a popular stop for road trippers. The smugglers museum has a separate entry fee.

ad.cta_label: Find a stay in Bodmin Moor

facts.one_liner: A Bloomsbury pub keeping its rare Victorian ‘snob screens’ around the bar.
facts.why_go: Built in the 1720s and refurbished in the Victorian era, The Lamb on Lamb’s Conduit Street is one of the few pubs that still has its swivelling etched-glass ‘snob screens’, which let well-off drinkers avoid being seen by bar staff. Dark wood, photographs of music-hall stars and a polyphon music box give it great character; Charles Dickens lived nearby.
facts.best_time: Weekday afternoons; the street is pleasant for strolling in good weather.
facts.how_to_get_there: Russell Square and Holborn stations are both about 8 minutes’ walk.
facts.good_to_know: Pair with a visit to the Charles Dickens Museum on nearby Doughty Street.

facts.one_liner: One of Belfast’s oldest pubs, with whitewashed walls and traditional music.
facts.why_go: Kelly’s Cellars on Bank Street dates from 1720, making it one of Belfast’s oldest pubs. It is resolutely old-fashioned—vaulted ceiling, elbow-worn bar and walls crammed with memorabilia—and is known for traditional Irish music sessions and pub food. Tradition links it to the United Irishmen of the 1790s.
facts.best_time: Evenings and weekend afternoons for traditional music sessions.
facts.how_to_get_there: In Belfast city centre beside the Castlecourt shopping centre, a short walk from City Hall.
facts.good_to_know: Sessions are informal—check locally which nights have music.

facts.one_liner: A narrow Victorian bar of mirrors and mahogany on Fleet Street.
facts.why_go: The Palace Bar has stood on Fleet Street since 1823 and keeps a classic Victorian interior of mahogany, etched mirrors and a skylit back room. It was long a haunt of Irish Times journalists and writers such as Patrick Kavanagh and Flann O’Brien, and it remains one of Dublin’s best-loved traditional pubs, just steps from Temple Bar.
facts.best_time: Weekday afternoons for a quiet pint; evenings are lively.
facts.how_to_get_there: On Fleet Street, a short walk from Trinity College and O’Connell Bridge.
facts.good_to_know: It has an upstairs whiskey bar. No TVs or loud music downstairs—this is a talking pub.

facts.one_liner: A Victorian Dublin pub with its old grocer’s drawers still behind the bar.
facts.why_go: Toner’s on Lower Baggot Street is one of Dublin’s classic Victorian pubs, with its original shop-front drawers and shelves from its days as a grocer-pub, stone floor and snug. Tradition has it that W. B. Yeats drank here—reputedly the only pub he ever visited—and it has a large courtyard for summer evenings.
facts.best_time: Any time; summer evenings for the courtyard.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 10 minutes’ walk from St Stephen’s Green on Baggot Street.
facts.good_to_know: The Yeats story is a tradition rather than documented history. Busy on match days.

facts.one_liner: A thatch-era country pub beside the walls of Bunratty Castle.
facts.why_go: Durty Nelly’s sits by the bridge at the foot of 15th-century Bunratty Castle, and claims to date from 1620. Low ceilings, open fires, traditional music and a riverside setting make it one of Ireland’s most famous country pubs, and the castle’s medieval banquets and folk park are right next door.
facts.best_time: Year-round; summer evenings for music, winter for fireside pints.
facts.how_to_get_there: In Bunratty village off the N18, about 15 minutes by car from Shannon Airport and 20 minutes from Limerick.
facts.good_to_know: Combine with a medieval banquet at Bunratty Castle (book ahead).

facts.one_liner: A painted corner pub in Galway’s Latin Quarter, buzzing with music and chat.
facts.why_go: Tigh Neachtáin (Naughton’s) has been a pub since 1894 on the corner of Quay Street and Cross Street, in a building once home to Richard ‘Humanity Dick’ Martin, the animal-welfare campaigner. Its colourful façade, snugs and wooden nooks make it a hub of Galway life, with traditional music sessions and a strong whiskey selection.
facts.best_time: Summer for street life and festivals (Galway Arts Festival in July); winter evenings for snug sessions.
facts.how_to_get_there: In the pedestrian Latin Quarter, about 10 minutes’ walk from Galway Ceannt station.
facts.good_to_know: Seats are scarce on festival nights; arrive early afternoon to grab a snug.

facts.why_go: Near the Galeries Royales Saint-Hubert, À la Mort Subite has occupied this spot since 1928 and its long hall of mirrors, wooden benches and cream walls is protected heritage (listed in 1998). It gave its name to the Mort Subite lambic and gueuze beers, and is a classic stop for a kriek with cheese or a tartine.
facts.best_time: Afternoons any time of year.
facts.how_to_get_there: A few minutes’ walk from the Grand-Place and Bruxelles-Central station.
facts.good_to_know: Waiters in traditional aprons take orders at the table. Try a gueuze or kriek.

facts.one_liner: A Benedictine hilltop monastery brewing beer above the Ammersee.
facts.why_go: Andechs Abbey crowns the ‘Holy Mountain’ east of the Ammersee lake, a pilgrimage site with a flamboyant Baroque church and a monastery brewery whose profits support the monks’ work. The Bräustüberl and beer garden serve its beers with Bavarian food and long views over the Alpine foothills. Composer Carl Orff is buried in the church.
facts.best_time: May–October for the beer garden; weekdays are quieter than sunny weekends.
facts.how_to_get_there: Take the S-Bahn from Munich to Herrsching (about 50 minutes), then walk up through the Kiental gorge (about 1 hour) or take the bus.
facts.good_to_know: Bring cash for convenience; it gets very busy on summer weekends and holidays.

facts.one_liner: Budapest’s original ruin bar, a maze of salvaged junk and fairy lights.
facts.why_go: Szimpla Kert pioneered Budapest’s ‘ruin bars’ (romkocsma) in the Jewish Quarter: a crumbling building filled with mismatched furniture, old bathtubs, a Trabant car and layers of art. It has grown into a community hub with live music, film screenings and a Sunday farmers’ market, and rooms full of graffiti and plants to explore.
facts.best_time: Sunday mornings for the farmers’ market; late evenings for the full party atmosphere.
facts.how_to_get_there: On Kazinczy utca in District VII, a short walk from Astoria or Deák Ferenc tér metro stations.
facts.good_to_know: Be mindful of residents when leaving late. Queues form on weekend nights.

facts.one_liner: A 17th-century canal-corner brown café famous for its apple pie.
facts.why_go: On the corner of the Prinsengracht and Brouwersgracht, Papeneiland has been a café since 1642, making it one of Amsterdam’s oldest ‘brown cafés’. Delft tiles, a wood stove and a tiny interior keep it cosy, and its apple pie is a local favourite. Legend says a tunnel once connected it to a hidden Catholic church across the canal.
facts.best_time: Mornings or early afternoons for pie and coffee; quiet weekday evenings.
facts.how_to_get_there: In the Jordaan, about 10 minutes’ walk from Amsterdam Centraal.
facts.good_to_know: Seating is limited; on fine days, sit outside facing the canals.
